title: Scientists Find a Tiny New Tiger Cat
summary:
Scientists have found a brand-new tiger cat! It is called Leopardus tilcayo and lives in Bolivia. It is the first new living cat species described in more than 100 years.

These tiny cats have slim bodies, spotted fur, and ringed tails. They weigh about two kilograms (4.4 pounds), about as much as a four-month-old pet kitten. They seem to live in the Yungas forests of the central Andes Mountains.

Scientists named it in the October 5 issue of Current Biology. The last new living cat species was the Uruguayan pampas cat, described in 1923.

Jonas Lescroart and his team studied the genes of 38 Leopardus species. They expected two to four kinds of tiger cats, but found five — one never described before.

The proof came from two cats at a Bolivian wildlife shelter: a female treated for injuries and set free, and a male named Tigrino who still lives there. Cat expert Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz noticed Tigrino looked different and tested his genes.

Scientists still do not know how many of these tiny cats live in the wild.
why_it_matters: Finding a new species shows there are still animals to discover, and knowing about them helps people protect the forests they live in.

keywords.explanation: A species is a kind of animal or plant, like a tiger or a rose.
Genes are tiny instructions inside living things that decide how they grow and look.
The Yungas are forests on the sides of mountains in South America.
The Andes Mountains are a long chain of tall mountains in South America.
A wildlife shelter is a place that cares for wild animals that are hurt or need help.

Scientists study genes, the tiny instructions inside living things, to tell whether animals belong to the same species or a new one.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists led by Jonas Lescroart, cat expert Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, and two cats at a Bolivian wildlife shelter.
WHAT: Scientists found and described a brand-new tiger cat species, Leopardus tilcayo.
WHERE: In the Yungas forests of the central Andes Mountains in Bolivia.
WHY: Gene tests showed the cats were different from all other known tiger cats.
